variables.meaning: the speed of light in a vacuum, 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s, the same for every observer whatever the motion of the source
the relative velocity between two observers, or of a moving clock, ship or particle relative to an observer
the relativistic factor, 1/√(1 − v²/c²), which is 1 at rest and grows without limit as v approaches c
the proper time, the elapsed time measured by an observer at rest relative to the event being observed
the elapsed time for the same event measured by an observer moving relative to it, longer than the proper time
the width of the astronaut’s ship, which light crosses once each way in her frame
the length of one slanted leg of the light’s path as seen from the Earth
the proper length, the distance between two points measured by an observer at rest relative to both of them
the contracted length, the length measured by an observer moving relative to the object, shorter than the proper length
the velocity of an object relative to one observer
the velocity of the same object relative to the other observer, who moves at v relative to the first
the wavelength of electromagnetic radiation as emitted by its source
the wavelength of the same radiation as received by an observer moving relative to the source
the frequency of the radiation as emitted by its source
the frequency of the radiation as received by the observer
the rest mass of an object, its mass measured by an observer at rest relative to it
the relativistic momentum, γmu, which approaches infinity as u approaches c
the total energy of an object, γmc²
the rest energy of an object, mc², the energy it has when it is not moving
the relativistic kinetic energy, (γ − 1)mc², the part of the total energy due to motion
the classical kinetic energy, ½mv², which agrees with the relativistic value only at low velocities
the net work done on an object, which goes into its kinetic energy
a change in rest mass, the mass gained when energy is stored or destroyed when energy is released

glossary.definition: the study of how different observers measure the same event
the theory that, in an inertial frame of reference, the motion of an object is relative to the frame from which it is viewed or measured
a reference frame in which a body at rest remains at rest and a body in motion moves at a constant speed in a straight line unless acted on by an outside force
the idea that the laws of physics are the same and can be stated in their simplest form in all inertial frames of reference
the idea that the speed of light $c$ is a constant, independent of the source
an investigation performed in 1887 that proved that the speed of light in a vacuum is the same in all frames of reference from which it is viewed
the phenomenon of time passing slower to an observer who is moving relative to another observer

$\Delta t_0$. the time measured by an observer at rest relative to the event being observed: $\Delta t=\frac{\Delta t_0}{\sqrt{1-\frac{v^{2}}{c^{2}}}}=\gamma\Delta t_0$, where $\gamma=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\frac{v^{2}}{c^{2}}}}$

this asks why a twin traveling at a relativistic speed away and then back towards the Earth ages less than the Earth-bound twin. The premise to the paradox is faulty because the traveling twin is accelerating, and special relativity does not apply to accelerating frames of reference

$L_0$; the distance between two points measured by an observer who is at rest relative to both of the points; Earth-bound observers measure proper length when measuring the distance between two points that are stationary relative to the Earth
$L$, the shortening of the measured length of an object moving relative to the observer’s frame: $L=L_0\sqrt{1-\frac{v^{2}}{c^{2}}}=\frac{L_0}{\gamma}$

the method of adding velocities when $v \ll c$; velocities add like regular numbers in one-dimensional motion: $u=v+u'$, where $v$ is the velocity between two observers, $u$ is the velocity of an object relative to one observer, and $u'$ is the velocity relative to the other observer

the method of adding velocities of an object moving at a relativistic speed: $u=\frac{v+u'}{1+\frac{vu'}{c^{2}}}$, where $v$ is the relative velocity between two observers, $u$ is the velocity of an object relative to one observer, and $u'$ is the velocity relative to the other observer

a change in wavelength of radiation that is moving relative to the observer; the wavelength of the radiation is longer (called a red shift) than that emitted by the source when the source moves away from the observer and shorter (called a blue shift) when the source moves toward the observer; the shifted wavelength is described by the equation $\lambda_{\text{obs}}=\lambda_{\text{s}}\sqrt{\frac{1+\frac{u}{c}}{1-\frac{u}{c}}}$ where $\lambda_{\text{obs}}$ is the observed wavelength, $\lambda_{\text{s}}$ is the source wavelength, and $u$ is the velocity of the source to the observer

$p$, the momentum of an object moving at relativistic velocity; $p=\gamma mu$, where $m$ is the rest mass of the object, $u$ is its velocity relative to an observer, and the relativistic factor $\gamma=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\frac{u^{2}}{c^{2}}}}$
the mass of an object as measured by a person at rest relative to the object
the energy stored in an object at rest: $E_0=mc^{2}$
the kinetic energy of an object moving at relativistic speeds: $\text{KE}_{\text{rel}}=(\gamma-1)mc^{2}$, where $\gamma=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\frac{v^{2}}{c^{2}}}}$
